conclusions: torch CPU generation is thread-count insensitive on this short fixture: 1/2/4/8 threads all land within 1.53-1.57 s.
fast decode is a stable ~1.20x speedup over reference decode on this fixture with identical events.
torch.compile on this Apple CPU path is far slower (~6.6 s vs ~1.56 s); --compile-decode is not a CPU gain here.
bf16 autocast on this Apple CPU path is ~2.2x slower than fp32 (3.37 s vs 1.56 s) and produced identical events; it is not a CPU speedup.
MLX beats torch CPU on a 100 s song at batch-size 64 (18.6-28.3 s vs ~41 s) and is slower at batch-size 1.
inference_mode replaced no_grad on the decode entry points: 100 s song median 40.995 s vs 41.755 s (n=3 each, ~1.8% faster) with identical events.
Every backend produced the same event multiset on both fixtures when hashed with the repository's note_hash.
On the 100 s song, 1-8 CPU threads and 1-8 interop threads all land within 2%; raising the thread count is not a CPU speedup on this Apple host.
Model construction on meta + assign=True cut weight loading from 1.338 s to ~0.52 s with bit-identical parameters.
int8 dynamic quantization is unavailable on the Apple ARM PyTorch 2.15.0 build (NoQEngine); x86_64 may differ and must be measured there.
x86_64 (AMD EPYC 9V74, 4 vCPU): 2 CPU threads were fastest on the synthetic 8 s fixture (17.49 s vs 18.55 s at 1 and 20.13 s at 4); thread tuning is host-specific, unlike the flat Apple ARM result.
Same synthetic fixture, same weights: Apple ARM64 ~4.8 s vs x86_64 4-vCPU runner 17.5-20.1 s, byte-identical events. Different hardware classes, same input.
